The auto selector and racing

Source: vignettes/auto-selector.Rmd
auto-selector.Rmd
library(optimix)

Why

An agronomist running the same nitrogen-response cost surface across dozens of trial sites does not want to hand-pick a different optimiser for each site, and she does not want to trust a single fixed choice either, because no optimiser wins everywhere. Rice framed this in 1976 as the algorithm-selection problem: pick, per problem instance, the portfolio member that will perform best. method = "auto" is the optimix answer. It reads what the problem declares (design space, noise, expense, budget), commits to an engine, and records the decision in the result, so the agronomist gets one call that works out, site by site, which optimiser to trust, and a written reason she can check.

What

.auto_select() (reached through method = "auto", optimix’s default) runs in two tiers. Tier 1 is a transparent rule read straight off what the problem declares – no extra evaluations spent. Tier 3 escalates to racing: a short trial for each installed candidate engine, then the remaining budget committed to the trial leader. Every result carries a provenance list recording the engine that ran, why it was chosen, and which tier decided; a raced result additionally keeps the trial scores in provenance$race. method = "race" reaches the same racing machinery directly, skipping the tier-1 deliberation.

Do

The objective

The examples below use a shifted multimodal test function, a synthetic Rastrigin-style surface whose global minimum sits at 1.3 in each coordinate:

shifted <- function(x) {
  z <- x - 1.3
  sum(z^2 - 10 * cos(2 * pi * z) + 10)
}

Engines available on this build

Three sections below need an optional engine each, or a pair of them: GenSA for the noisy-objective rule and every race, cmaes alongside it for racing specifically, and nloptr (for nloptr_bobyqa) for the budget-sweep figure. Each guarded chunk checks for what it needs and prints one sentence in its place when an engine is missing.

has_gensa <- requireNamespace("GenSA", quietly = TRUE)
has_cmaes <- requireNamespace("cmaes", quietly = TRUE)
has_nloptr <- requireNamespace("nloptr", quietly = TRUE)
has_ggplot2 <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
race_ok <- has_gensa && has_cmaes
sweep_ok <- race_ok && has_nloptr && has_ggplot2

Tier 1: the rules

When the problem’s declaration already determines a good choice, auto applies a transparent rule and spends no evaluations on selection. A noisy objective goes to a noise-tolerant global engine. An expensive objective goes to Bayesian optimisation, which spends few true evaluations. A permutation design space goes to the native simulated annealer, described in Combinatorial optimisation and delta evaluation. And a small budget stays with the rules, because probing the landscape would eat too much of it. A noisy objective also never races – ranking engines on one short noisy trial each would rank them on luck – so its rule commits directly:

noisy_prob <- optim_problem(
  fn = function(x) sum(x^2) + rnorm(1, sd = 0.05),
  space = space_box(lower = c(-3, -3), upper = c(3, 3)),
  objective = objective_noisy(sd = 0.05),
  max_evals = 500, seed = 42
)
res_noisy <- optimix(noisy_prob)
res_noisy$provenance[c("engine", "why", "tier")]
#> $engine
#> [1] "gensa"
#> 
#> $why
#> [1] "noisy objective: gensa (noise-tolerant global)"
#> 
#> $tier
#> [1] 1

Tier 3: racing

For a deterministic objective with an ample budget, auto escalates from rules to evidence. It samples the landscape once with a Latin-hypercube design, gives each installed candidate engine a short trial from the best sampled point as a shared warm start, and commits the remaining budget to the trial leader, warm-started from the leader’s own best. The landscape sample and every trial evaluation are charged against the budget, and the final run receives only what is left.

set.seed(1)
res <- optimix(shifted, lower = c(-5, -5), upper = c(5, 5))
res
#> <optimix_result>
#>   optimiser : gensa
#>   value     : 0
#>   par       : 1.3, 1.3
#>   evals     : 2000
#>   converged : yes
res$provenance[c("engine", "tier", "why")]
#> $engine
#> [1] "gensa"
#> 
#> $tier
#> [1] 3
#> 
#> $why
#> [1] "race 3 engines (ELA quad R2 = 0.62); gensa led the race"
res$provenance$race
#>         gensa         cmaes nloptr_bobyqa 
#>   0.000000000   0.001694246   0.000000000

The provenance is how a result explains itself: the engine that ran (engine), why it was chosen (why), and which tier decided (tier is 1 for a rule and 3 for a race). A raced result also keeps the trial scores.

Asking for a race directly

method = "race" skips the deliberation and races the installed global engines immediately. It needs a continuous box space and at least two installed candidates:

set.seed(2)
raced <- optimix(shifted, lower = c(-5, -5), upper = c(5, 5),
                 method = "race")
raced$provenance$why
#> [1] "explicit race of 3 engines; gensa led the race"

Budgets are respected

max_evals caps the true objective evaluations – a soft cap, since an engine may finish the internal step it is in – and the reported count is the true total across every stage of the search. A budget of 200 is too small for a race here (the landscape sample alone would cost a quarter of it), so auto stays with the tier-1 rule; when the chunk below executes, capped$counts[["function"]] sits at or just above 200, confirming the cap was honoured rather than silently overrun:

set.seed(3)
capped <- optimix(shifted, lower = c(-5, -5), upper = c(5, 5),
                  max_evals = 200)
capped$provenance$tier
#> [1] 1
capped$counts[["function"]]
#> [1] 200

Why the race commits to a leader

A single race, run once, shows which engine won; it does not show how the three race candidates behave as the budget grows, which is the reason the tier-3 rule commits the remaining budget to the trial leader rather than splitting it evenly. The sweep below re-solves the same shifted surface with each of gensa, cmaes, and nloptr_bobyqa directly, at six budgets from 30 to 1000 evaluations, and records the best value each reaches:

sweep_budgets <- c(30L, 60L, 120L, 250L, 500L, 1000L)
sweep_engines <- c("gensa", "cmaes", "nloptr_bobyqa")
sweep_grid <- expand.grid(
  engine = sweep_engines, budget = sweep_budgets, stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
s1 <- nrow(sweep_grid)
sweep_rows <- vector("list", s1)
for (i1 in seq_len(s1)) {
  prob_i <- optim_problem(
    fn = shifted, space = space_box(lower = c(-5, -5), upper = c(5, 5)),
    max_evals = sweep_grid$budget[i1], seed = 5
  )
  res_i <- optimix(prob_i, method = sweep_grid$engine[i1])
  sweep_rows[[i1]] <- data.frame(
    engine = sweep_grid$engine[i1], budget = sweep_grid$budget[i1],
    value = res_i$value, evals = res_i$counts[["function"]]
  )
} # ends i1, over the engine x budget grid
sweep_df <- do.call(rbind, sweep_rows)
sweep_df
#>           engine budget        value evals
#> 1          gensa     30 9.949591e-01    91
#> 2          cmaes     30 8.026175e+00    30
#> 3  nloptr_bobyqa     30 1.989918e+00    32
#> 4          gensa     60 9.949591e-01    91
#> 5          cmaes     60 5.441800e+00    60
#> 6  nloptr_bobyqa     60 1.989918e+00    40
#> 7          gensa    120 9.949591e-01   120
#> 8          cmaes    120 1.348760e+00   120
#> 9  nloptr_bobyqa    120 1.989918e+00    40

#> 11         cmaes    250 9.954714e-01   246
#> 12 nloptr_bobyqa    250 1.989918e+00    40

Best value each engine reaches by the largest budget in the sweep (1000 evaluations).
engine budget value evals
gensa 1000 0.0000 1000
cmaes 1000 0.9950 996
nloptr_bobyqa 1000 1.9899 40 
ggplot2::ggplot(
  sweep_df, ggplot2::aes(x = evals, y = value, colour = engine)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_viridis_d(name = "engine") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "true objective evaluations",
    y = "best value found",
    title = "Convergence of the three raced engines, by budget"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()

Best value found against the true evaluation budget, for the three engines the tier-3 race chooses between. nloptr_bobyqa (a local search) settles early and stops improving regardless of budget; cmaes and gensa keep improving as the budget grows, with gensa reaching the global optimum by budget 500. This is what a single race’s trial-then-commit step is racing for.

The evidence

The comparison is against zakharov, salomon, and bohachevsky – three functions held out from the rules auto was designed against – each run at 3 dimensions x 6 seeds x 2 budgets (n = 54 instances per budget). These figures come from the package’s own tier-2/tier-3 held-out validation study and are not recomputed in this vignette. On that held-out set auto beat the best fixed single engine (gensa) where it matters most: at a constrained budget of 300 evaluations per dimension it solved more instances (success 0.63 against 0.56) at better median quality and lower cost. At a generous budget of 1000 evaluations per dimension it matched the single-best engine’s quality (an equal-or-tighter median gap) with about forty per cent fewer evaluations, but its success rate trails single-best’s at that budget (0.685 against 0.759) – racing spends part of the budget on trials that a strong single global would have spent solving, which costs a little when nearly every instance already favours that one engine. The efficiency win is real; the generous-budget success rate is the price paid for it.

A feature-based shortcut – route problems that look smooth to a cheap local solver – was prototyped and rejected on the same held-out evidence: one function is multimodal yet looks perfectly quadratic to a coarse sample (a bowl hiding a cosine ripple), so no feature threshold routes it safely. Racing is feature-free, resolving such cases by actually trying the engines, and that is why the escalation is a race rather than a landscape heuristic.

Read

The noisy-objective rule commits to gensa at tier 1 with no race, matching the stated rule: a noisy objective is never raced.

On the deterministic shifted surface, the tier-3 race commits to gensa (tier 3), reaching a value of 0 against a trial score of 0 for that same engine’s own short trial – on this instance the short trial alone had already located the exact optimum, so the remaining budget confirmed rather than improved that answer – not every race needs its commit step to do further work. The explicit race (method = "race") reasons the same way: explicit race of 3 engines; gensa led the race. At a budget of 200, too small for a race, auto stays with the tier-1 rule (tier 1), and 200 evaluations were spent against that cap – at or just above 200, confirming the budget was honoured rather than silently overrun.

The sweep makes the reason for that commit-to-the-leader design visible: nloptr_bobyqa stops improving once its own local search declares convergence, spending only 32-40 true evaluations regardless of how large a budget it is offered, and settling on a value well short of the global optimum. cmaes and gensa both keep using every evaluation they are given and keep improving; gensa is the first to reach the global optimum, at a budget of 500 evaluations. A single short trial (the race’s own first step) could not have shown this – only a sweep across budgets does – which is exactly why the race commits the remaining budget to whichever engine’s short trial led, rather than trusting the trial’s ranking to hold at every budget.

Limits

The sweep above re-solves one synthetic surface at one seed; it shows the shape of three engines’ convergence on that instance, not a general ranking, and the held-out study cited in The evidence is what actually supports the claim that auto beats a fixed single engine on average. The race itself commits on the strength of a single short trial per candidate, which is why .auto_select() never races a noisy objective – a single-trial ranking on noise would rank engines on luck rather than performance, and nothing in this vignette exercises that failure mode directly. Every example here is a continuous box in two or three dimensions; permutation spaces route around racing entirely, to the native annealer covered in Combinatorial optimisation and delta evaluation.

What to read next

Getting started with optimix covers the two front doors and the result object this vignette assumes throughout. Mapping optima and the orchestra manifest covers goal = "map", a different axis of the same selector, including what happens when no installed engine can honour the request. Combinatorial optimisation and delta evaluation covers the one design space auto never races: permutations, routed instead to a dedicated annealer.

Reproduce

Seed 42 for the noisy-objective example, 1 for the race, 2 for the explicit race, 3 for the budget cap, and 5 for every run in the budget sweep.
